# Introduction

This course is a clean, self-contained explanation of **Hoare logic** and related deductive techniques for reasoning about programs. It is based on the notes you provided (where you used `m` to denote the program memory state instead of the usual $\mu$), expanded with clarifications, proofs, and worked examples. The file is a Quarto `.qmd` document configured to render to PDF using the LuTeX engine.

We assume a small imperative language with integers and booleans, assignments, sequencing, conditionals, loops, and function calls. No explicit memory management is considered (no heaps, pointers, or allocation).

# 1. Programs, specifications and correctness

A *program* is a finite sequence of instructions written in our small language. A *specification* describes what the program is supposed to compute; we focus on **functional properties**, expressed as formulas of first-order logic (FOL).

A common way to specify a program fragment $c$ is a **Hoare triple**
$$
\{P\}\; c\; \{Q\}
$$

where $P$ (precondition) and $Q$ (postcondition) are logical predicates over program variables.

**Meaning.** The triple $\{P\}\; c\; \{Q\}$ is *valid* iff for every memory state $m$, if $m \models P$ and the execution of $c$ from $m$ terminates producing state $m'$, then $m' \models Q$.

# 2. Memory and semantics

We model the program memory as a function:
$$
m : Var \to \mathbb{Z} \cup \{\text{tt}, \text{ff}\}.
$$

We define two semantic functions:

- $Val(e, m)$: evaluates expression $e$ in state $m$.
- $Mem(c, m)$: state after executing command $c$ from state $m$.

Notation: $m[x \leftarrow v]$ means the same as $m$, except $x$ now maps to $v$.

Example: $Mem(x := t, m) = m[x \leftarrow Val(t,m)]$.

# 3. Axioms and rules of Hoare logic

## 3.1 Assignment axiom

$$
\{Q[x \leftarrow t]\}\; x := t\; \{Q\}
$$

## 3.2 Consequence, sequencing, conditional, and while rules

| Rule | Formulation |
|------|--------------|
| **Consequence** | If $P' \Rightarrow P$, $\{P\}\; c\; \{Q\}$ and $Q \Rightarrow Q'$, then $\{P'\}\; c\; \{Q'\}$. |
| **Sequence** | If $\{P\}\; c_1\; \{R\}$ and $\{R\}\; c_2\; \{Q\}$, then $\{P\}\; c_1; c_2\; \{Q\}$. |
| **Conditional** | If $\{P \land b\}\; c_1\; \{Q\}$ and $\{P \land \lnot b\}\; c_2\; \{Q\}$, then $\{P\}\; \text{if } b \text{ then } c_1 \text{ else } c_2\; \{Q\}$. |
| **While** | If $\{I \land b\}\; c\; \{I\}$, then $\{I\}\; \text{while } b \text{ do } c\; \{I \land \lnot b\}$. |

```{=latex}
\draw[dashed] (q.south) -- (triple.north east);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

# 4. Weakest precondition (WP)

The weakest precondition $WP(c,Q)$ is the least predicate $P$ such that $\{P\}\; c\; \{Q\}$ holds.

$$
WP(x := t, Q) = Q[x \leftarrow t]
$$

$$
WP(c_1; c_2, Q) = WP(c_1, WP(c_2, Q))
$$

$$
WP(\text{if } b \text{ then } c_1 \text{ else } c_2, Q) =
(b \Rightarrow WP(c_1,Q)) \land (\lnot b \Rightarrow WP(c_2,Q))
$$

### Example TikZ — WP propagation

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.5cm,>=stealth,thick]
\node (q) {$Q$};
\node[below=of q] (wp2) {$WP(c_2, Q)$};
\node[below=of wp2] (wp1) {$WP(c_1, WP(c_2, Q))$};
\node[left=of wp1] (p) {$P$};
\draw[->] (wp2) -- (q) node[midway, right] {$c_2$};
\draw[->] (wp1) -- (wp2) node[midway, right] {$c_1$};
\draw[->, dashed] (p) -- (wp1);
\node[right=1.5cm of q] {Backward reasoning flow};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

# 5. Loops and invariants

An *invariant* $I$ satisfies:
$$
\{I \land b\}\; c\; \{I\}.
$$

When the loop exits, $(I \land \lnot b) \Rightarrow Q$ should hold.

### Example TikZ — Loop structure

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.8cm,>=stealth,thick]
\node (start) [draw, rounded corners] {Entry: $I$};
\node[below=of start] (cond) [draw, diamond, aspect=2, inner sep=2pt] {$b$};
\node[below left=1.2cm and 1.5cm of cond] (body) [draw, rounded corners] {Body $c$};
\node[below right=1.2cm and 1.5cm of cond] (exit) [draw, rounded corners] {Exit: $\lnot b \land I$};
\draw[->] (start) -- (cond);
\draw[->] (cond) -- node[left] {true} (body);
\draw[->] (cond) -- node[right] {false} (exit);
\draw[->] (body) |- (cond);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

# 6. Example proofs

### Example 1: addition loop invariant

```text
res := a;
aux := b;
while aux > 0 do
  res := res + 1;
  aux := aux - 1;
done
```
Invariant: $res + aux = a + b \land aux \ge 0$.

### Example TikZ — Proof structure

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.8cm,>=stealth,thick]
\node (pre) [draw, rounded corners] {$I$};
\node[below=of pre] (cond) [draw, diamond, aspect=2, inner sep=2pt] {$aux > 0$};
\node[below left=1.2cm and 1.4cm of cond] (body) [draw, rounded corners] {Body: $res:=res+1; aux:=aux-1$};
\node[below right=1.2cm and 1.4cm of cond] (post) [draw, rounded corners] {$I \land \lnot(aux>0)$};
\draw[->] (pre) -- (cond);
\draw[->] (cond) -- node[left] {true} (body);
\draw[->] (cond) -- node[right] {false} (post);
\draw[->] (body) |- (cond);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

# 7. Summary

- Hoare logic = logical reasoning about programs.  
- Key constructs: triples, inference rules, invariants, variants.  
- Proofs can be automated via weakest precondition generation.
